title: How Steve Jobs learned from Robert Noyce: cold-calling legends and hiring smarter people
summary: In a 2003 interview, Jobs reflects on his mentor Robert Noyce, the "soul of Intel." He explains how he cold-called Valley legends for lunch, why a senior leader's job is recruiting, direction and inspiration rather than doing the work, why optimism and passion sustain innovation, and why history and succession matter.

principles.text: Cold-call the people you admire and ask to learn from them; most will say yes.
principles.quote: I just called them up and I said, “Look, I’m young and I’m trying to run with this company. I’m just wondering if I could buy you lunch once a quarter and pick your brain.”

principles.text: Hire people smarter than you, including younger ones, instead of doing their work.
principles.quote: If you’re smart, you’re hiring twenty-five-year-olds who are smarter than you. You know things that they don’t know, and they know things that you don’t know, and it all works.

principles.text: A leader's job is to recruit, set direction, and inspire, not design the product.
principles.quote: His job was to, number one, recruit; number two, set an overall direction; and number three, you know, inspire and cajole and persuade.

principles.text: Innovation needs optimism and real passion, because it is extremely hard.
principles.quote: It’s optimism and passion, because it’s really hard. And if you don’t really, really care about what you’re doing, you’re gonna give up if you’re a sane person

principles.text: To understand the present you must understand how it got here; there is humanity under the dry history.
principles.quote: There’s a human drama to most everything. You look at it sometimes, and it seems dry as history. But if you peel the onion, there’s humanity underneath.

principles.text: Great leaders plan succession and let go, so the company is not a one-man show.
principles.quote: He understood how important it was to have a succession, to keep the company going, not have it just be a one-man show.
